title: Maps and Places
objectives: I can name the parts of a map and a globe.
I can use a symbol, a direction, and a landmark to find a place.
I can tell a route and the distance between two places.
I can use the words to tell a friend how to get somewhere.
rationale: Maps are the main social-studies text of second grade, and these words let children read one and describe how to get from one place to another. The eight words split into tools for finding places (map, globe), the parts of a map that carry information (symbol, direction, landmark), and the ideas about getting somewhere (route, distance, border). Children draw a map of the classroom or the school yard and use the words to tell a partner how to find an object. The unit revisits diagram, label, half, and deep, which show up in map keys, map scales, and the oceans on a globe.

passage.title: Sam Reads a Map
paras: Sam looked at a map of his town. A star was the symbol for the library. He chose a route past the tall clock tower, a landmark he could see from far away.
The distance was half a mile, and the direction was north. A river made the border of his town. Back home, Sam spun a globe to find his town on Earth.

qs.q: What does "landmark" mean in the story?
choices: a place that is easy to recognize
qs.why: Sam could see the tall clock tower from far away, so a landmark is a place that is easy to recognize.

qs.q: What was the symbol for the library?
qs.why: The story says a star was the symbol for the library.
The story says the distance was half a mile.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight words for reading and talking about maps. Use a real map of the school, the class, or the town, and a classroom globe. Children draw their own map with symbols and use direction words. Revisit diagram, label, half, and deep: a map is a diagram with labels, and a globe shows half the Earth at a time.

notes.va.map.n: A map shows where places are. Start with a map of the room. Children may think a map is only for roads; show a map of a park or a school.
notes.va.globe.n: A globe is a round model of Earth. Show land and water and point out that water covers most of the surface. A flat map cannot show the shape of Earth without stretching.
notes.va.direction.n: Teach the compass directions north, south, east, west, and also left and right. Teach only the way something is facing here. Directions can also mean steps for doing something; that second sense is not taught here.
notes.va.symbol.n: A symbol is a small picture that stands for something. Use the map key. Contrast with a label: a label is a word; a symbol is a picture.
notes.va.landmark.n: A landmark is a place or building that is easy to recognize. Use the school gate or a tall tree. Avoid tiny objects.
notes.va.route.n: A route is the path you take. Trace with a finger and say each turn. Children may say road for route; route is the path you choose. The sound is ROOT or ROWT; both are correct.
notes.va.distance.n: Distance is how far. Use steps or a ruler. Introduce the map scale in a simple way: one inch means one block.
notes.va.border.n: A border is the line between two places. Use a fence or a line on the floor. Keep the examples about towns, classrooms, and yards; avoid politically sensitive borders.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The map has a star. The key says a star is the symbol for the library. I want to go there. I will go north past the clock tower, because it is a landmark I can see. Then I turn right. That is my route.'
discuss: What is the best landmark near our school?
How does a symbol help a map stay small and clear?
misconceptions: Children may think a symbol is the real thing. A symbol stands for the real thing.
Some children confuse left and right on a map. Practice with a map on the floor.
Children may think a globe and a map are the same. A globe is round and keeps the true shape of Earth.
extend: Make a class map of the playground with symbols, a key, and a route.
Give oral directions to a hidden object using direction words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit diagram, label, half, and deep: a map is a diagram with labels, each label is a word for a place, a globe shows half the Earth at a time, and the oceans on a globe can be deep.

wida.oral: Give your partner directions to a hidden object in the room. Use a landmark and a direction word.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (mapa, globo terráqueo, dirección, símbolo, punto de referencia, ruta, distancia, frontera) not reviewed by a native speaker; punto de referencia for landmark has regional options such as hito.
Map facts used are general; no specific country or state border is claimed.
direction has a second sense (directions for doing something) that is not taught here.
